speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings that 1 initiate this debate to respond to the Senate's report on Bill C-22. First, this Bill is a carefully crafted package which balances a wide variety of interests. It reflects the need to respect in Canada, as in every other industrialized nation, the concept of intellectual property and that a creator, an inventor, an author, or whoever has created some property of value, is protected by the state from those who would copy that property.
It also reflects the fact that we in Canada must-I emphasize must-ensure that our research and development, science and technology activities are increased over what they have been in this country.
Everyone who has looked at science in Canada has concluded that we must do more. We cannot rely in perpetuity on our raw resources. We cannot continue with the philosophy that we can let the rest of the world develop the new technologies, the new drugs, the new treatments, and new goods and services, and we will pay for them with our raw resources. We cannot continue in that way without facing a drastic drop in our standard of living. We cannot continue our past practices in this country of being hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Bill C-22 also acknowledges that Canada ought to become involved in the manufacturing of fine chemicals, rather than relying on imported drugs and chemicals.
Most significantly, this package acknowledges that the health care of Canadians is vitally dependent on more research in health related areas in Canada. It makes common sense that only through research will we be able to increase the quality of
life of Canadians as our population gets older, and be able to find cures for Alzheimer's disease, arthritis, cancer, AIDS, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis and the many diseases that still inflict mankind. I think we all know intuitively that there is a much greater likelihood of getting the best and latest treatment in our hospitals if those physicians in our hospitals are working in a research-orientated atmosphere. If we are going to say in essence, let the Americans, Swiss, British, French and Germans do the medical research, we will wait until they prove out the new treatments, the new drugs, and then trust that our physicians will learn from their developments and apply those to Canadians, what we are saying is, Canadians will get the treatment later on. The rest of the world, the citizens of these other countries, will have access to these treatments early on.
Again, it is common sense-and everyone working in the area will acknowledge it-that physicians working in a research atmosphere are simply that much more able to understand, to diagnose quickly to realize the importance of new treatments and to apply them. There are all kinds of anecdotal support of that. Again, common sense and the normal experience all of us have had, would acknowledge that.
This package, Bill C-22, provides consumer protection. It provides that Canadians will have drug prices at 80 per cent of what they are in the United States. It provides that drugs will not increase more than the cost of living. It is in the original Bill C-22. It provides a mechanism to ensure that consumers are not gouged.
When one talks about consumers in Canada, one has to acknowledge first the magnificent health protection system we have. We have medicare. We have hospital care. No one in this country goes without medical help if they need it. No one in this country goes without drugs if they need them. Eighty-five per cent of the population is covered by drug plans. In fact, if one looks at the percentage of drugs prescribed under drug plans,one finds it is much higher than that. The 15 per cent who do not have drug plans are in a kind of low-risk group.
In my own personal experience, I had no drug plan until my first child arrived. When I was single and first married, I was young and healthy, and for the odd prescription I needed, it was simply economically sensible for me to pay for that prescription. When our children came along and it was necessary to have some protection in case of a debilitating disease the children might have had, I subscribed. That is the

August 21, 1987
Patent Act
nature of the situation. So when I talk about 85 per cent of the population having drug plans of one sort or another, in fact, way over 90 per cent of all drugs are purchased under drug plans.
Virtually 100 per cent of senior citizens in Canada are covered by drug plans and they are by far and away the largest users of drugs as a group. Therefore, consumers, individually, in Canada are already protected enormously. Bill C-22 ensures that the funders of those drug plans, be they provincial Governments, private plans and so on, will not be faced with increased costs as a result of this Bill.
It is a balanced package arrived at after months of discussions, negotiations, analysis and examination. Frankly, any objective, and I stress the word "objective", observer can reach no other conclusion after looking at all the facts.
Has this Bill been adequately studied? I do not know of a Bill, at least in this Parliament, which has had more study. This Bill had 87.5 hours of House and legislative committee time-87.5 hours. I do not know of any Bill which has had that much time. There were 250 submissions-250 submissions.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I find it strange to have it repeated in the House ad nauseam by Members of the Opposition that no one supports this Bill. Is there anyone involved in medical research, in the treatment of the sick in this country, who is not in
August 21, 1987

favour of this Bill? Is there anyone involved in the treatment of the sick in Canada who does not understand the importance of research and development? What about the experts? Is there anyone in that category who is not in favour of this Bill? I doubt it. That is not someone I would like to approach with an ailment, I will tell Hon. Members that.
How about the general public? The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) stated in his memo to the Liberal caucus: "Nobody supports this Bill". There was a poll taken of members of the Canadian public and the following question was put:
As you may know, the proposed bill would extend the period of time which brand-name companies are protected from having their drugs copied by generic companies . . . Those who support the Bill offer several arguments as to why it is necessary:
(1)	Companies which spend the money to develop new drugs should be protected from having their works copied just like any other invention.
(2)	If brand-name companies double research efforts in Canada, health care and quality of life will improve because of early access to new, high quality cures.
(3)	Canada is essentially a fair country and should be at least as fair to brand-name manufacturers as other countries are.
(4)	If we have to choose between developing research jobs in the brand-name companies or protecting existing jobs in generic companies, jobs in the brand-name companies would be better.
I could have developed much stronger arguments than those. But those are the arguments for it.
Those who oppose the Bill, the question goes on, offer several arguments as to why it is a bad idea:
(1)	Nothing should be done which might increase the price of drugs, because the sick and the poor will suffer.
We have heard that in the House many, many times from members of the Opposition.
(2)	Nothing should be done to help the brand-name companies which are mostly foreign-owned, especially if it hurts the Canadian-owned generic companies.
We have heard that before. It has been said that these foreign multinationals are the ones who will benefit.
(3)	Brand-name companies seem to be doing just fine in terms of profits, therefore, there is not a need to change things.
We heard that yesterday. Those companies are already getting profits so we should not change things.
(4)	Just because other countries offer greater protection to brand-name companies doesn't mean Canada is being unfair and needs to change its laws.
That is the "if it ain't broke then don't fix it" argument which we have heard from the other side.
What was the response of the public when asked, "Given those arguments how do you feel about it?" The arguments were interdispersed, sometimes leading with the positive and sometimes leading with the negative. Five per cent of the population said that the Bill is a very bad thing; 29 per cent
Patent Act
said it is a bad thing; 54 per cent said it is a good thing; and 8 per cent said it is a very good thing. So 62 per cent said it is a good thing, yet members of the Opposition say that the public of Canada does not support this measure. That is nonsense.

Perhaps more telling is this proposition:
I would support the bill if the government put in place a way of making sure that drug price increases would not be higher than the rate of inflation.
That is in fact in the law. We have done that. Eighty-one per cent said yes to that proposition, which means that 81 per cent of the Canadian population supports what we are doing in this Bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
What the amendments suggested by the other place in response to Bill C-22 would do would be to return to an old Liberal policy which has been thoroughly studied and found to be inadequate. I will point out very clearly in ways that can be subject to no other interpretation but to verify that they are inadequate. I will provide the evidence and the references on which the evidence can be checked if in fact there is doubt in people's minds.
First, the Senate proposals make a mockery of intellectual property protection. They fail to recognize the importance of intellectual property protection for developing both a dynamic pharmaceutical industry and new products. I find it incredible that there is not that understanding-I really do. People say, "We cannot provide patent protection because it might hurt the consumers". I will show that we protect the consumers. I ask Hon. Members to think about that argument.
If we were to allow generic book publishing; if we said that any time a book came out another company could publish a copy of it provided it paid the author a 4 per cent royalty, then when Pierre Berton comes out with his new book at $29.95 for the hard-cover copy, a generic producer could put out a paperback version immediately for $2.95. Think of the hundreds of millions of dollars that that would save Canadian consumers of books. Think what that would do to the intellectual quality of the country and to its literacy. Think about those people who, for unfortunate reasons, are unable to participate in athletic activities by virtue of age or infirmity and who rely on reading as their main source of recreation- the poor, the elderly and the infirm. Think of the money we would be saving them if we had generic book publishing. This would be an enormously beneficial thing to the consumer. But think of the destruction and havoc we would be wreaking on our authors.
Indeed, in this case, Pierre Berton is a millionaire already so why does he need any more copyright protection for his book? Is it not fair to consumers who want to read his excellent books about the history of Canada, the CPR, the Yukon and so on that they be able to get a generic copy immediately rather than

August 21, 1987
Patent Act
having to pay $29.95? I ask Hon. Members to think about that for a while, especially those who so casually dismiss the necessity of providing our scientists, researchers and those who discover cures with some kind of protection. Does it not make more sense that we say to our scientists, "Look, if you find a cure for cancer we will let you patent it and that is yours exclusively for 10 years; and if you get rich, alleluia"? Why is it a sin for a scientist to get rich on discovering a drug that cures cancer?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Name one rich scientist.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: How do we in Canada so casually and easily say that, by cracky, if that scientist is working for a company, well, we cannot allow that company to make profits. That is tragic. My goodness, if it is a company that employs that scientist, we cannot do that. 1 wonder about the values of a country that thinks that a million and a half dollars a year for Tim Raines is fair because he is a super athlete, but, by cracky, if a company discovers a life-saving drug and makes a big profit, then that is a catastrophe, a sin; that is immoral. Surely, if we are walking the moral high ground we say as a society, as we have said, "we will make sure that no one in this country goes without that cure for cancer. We as a society will pay for those cures. We will provide for the hospitalization, physician care and the drugs they need; but we will not penalize those who do the research and discover those life-saving drugs because we recognize that they have created something of value, some property, and they have a right to it. Surely that is the only moral high ground.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
1 heard the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) say, "Well, since it is mostly foreigners who have the patents in Canada, why should we protect these foreign patents? Only 5 per cent of the patents are Canadian". What that says is that it is all right to steal the intellectual property of foreigners. If in the process we steal the intellectual property of those 5 per cent of Canadians, well, that is the price we are willing to have those inventors pay. That is very magnanimous of us. We are prepared to see Canadian scientists carry the cost of our desire to take the intellectual property of foreigners.
That points out a symptom of what is wrong in this country. Only 5 per cent of our patents are by Canadians. That is a symptom of what the Government, and my colleague, the Minister of State (Science and Technology) (Mr. Oberle) have been repeatedly discussing. In fairness, it is also what the Opposition has been discussing. But when it comes to the specifics that will help, the Opposition says, "Oh, no. Yes, we are in favour of more science and technology, but do we recognize that the fruits of that effort should be patented? Oh, no". It is a source of continuous bewilderment to me how the Opposition manages to balance those two positions, or the
intellectual gymnastics they go through to occupy both those positions at one time.
This Bill states that there will be 10 years of exclusivity. Before the Bill was amended by the Senate, it provided that if the drug is developed in Canada there is a 20 year protection. What was taken out by the other place was a specific advantage for research done in Canada. That was taken out by the Liberals over there while the Liberals here state that there are not enough Canadian patents anyway, so why worry about it.
Time and time again, both here and elsewhere, I have faced the accusation that this is giving in to pressure from the United States. We have had pressure from the United States. We have also had pressure from Britain, France, Germany, Switzerland, Japan, and every single country in the western industrialized world. We are a member of the Group of Seven. We pride ourselves on being a major industrialized country. Yet, in our patent laws respecting pharmaceuticals, we are equivalent to Bolivia and Taiwan. The rest of the industrialized world does not understand that. They say that it is unconscionable for Canada to do that.
It is correct that we have been under pressure, and quite properly. If the Opposition thinks that we can retain our status as a leading industrialized country, retain our moral suasion capabilities vis-a-vis our allies, and still behave like a Third World country in terms of our treatment of intellectual property, I wonder what planet they come from. How can we possibly do that?
Even more important, at least to me, is that anybody who is even peripherally aware of what is happening in the world of science today recognizes that there is an enormous revolution in the area of biotechnology. Exciting things are happening that will have a profound effect on our society. It is vitally important that we participate. There are a number of small Canadian companies in this business. We have excellent universities that turn out excellent people. These people want to do research in this area, and they are ready to do it. But they cannot if we say that the fruits of their research are not patentable, or that the patent can be infringed upon through compulsory licence immediately. That is what we are saying, and we are giving a death knell to Canada's opportunities in this high-tech area. For goodness sakes, do not make this tragic mistake. Do not deal Canada out of this biotechnology revolution. Do not be so short-sighted for political gain.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Senate proposals contribute to the stagnation of pharmaceutical research development in Canada. Under our proposal we have a commitment from the industry, and it will be honoured because annually in the House of Commons we will have the figures to see if they have been honoured. If they have not been honoured, they will be reviewed and there will be an opportunity for redress during the review by Government in four years, and by Parliament in 10 years. There is a commitment for 10 per cent of sales to go
August 21, 1987

into research and development, which is the international norm for this industry. Based on projections of the growth in the drug market that will represent $1.4 billion in new investments by 1995.

In terms of jobs, increased research will make it possible to create about 3,000 jobs for Canadian graduates in advanced technology disciplines. Universities, hospitals and private research institutions across Canada will benefit from this increase.
Mr. Speaker, various scientific groups that carry out research across Canada have long awaited a Bill that would promote research in this country. Bill C-22 is that long-awaited legislation.
At public hearings held by the Senate Committee as well, these scientific groups all spoke out in favour of Bill C-22, as adopted by the House of Commons.

We have already had over $800 million announced, contingent upon passage of Bill C-22. That research will happen. It is false for the Opposition to claim that is not the case.
1 wish to refer the opposition critics to an article published last fall in the economic business supplement of le Devoir economique. In the article there are predictions by experts, and I will quote the headline:

"The new Patent Act could mean 10,000 jobs for Montreal."

According to the author, Franqois Cote, that predicts 1(3,000 employees in Montreal alone, based on spin-outs and development of related companies. For example, what is not included in the 3,000 jobs we are discussing are the several hundred jobs in manufacturing.
Incidentally, the Senate's amendments have made it impossible for a company called Delmar, in the City of LaSalle, which is apparently where Paul Martin Jr. will start his rise to greatness. I wonder if Paul Martin Jr. is aware that the Senate has put the kibosh on several tens of millions of dollars that were earmarked for the City of LaSalle for the manufacturing of fine chemicals. I wonder if he is aware of what his friends in Ottawa in the other place are doing to the city that at some future date he hopes to represent.
The fact of the matter is that the jobs are real, and they will occur. The Senate, and members of the Opposition, have stated that under the recommendation by the Senators, which they say is based on Eastman, the research fund has an incremental 10 per cent royalty on the generic companies. This is a type of tax because it does not go directly back to the owner, so it is not a royalty by definition. Under that 10 per cent it will create a royalty research fund which will be rebated
Patent Act
to companies that do research. They say that fund will guarantee research jobs. That is why they support it.
First, that does nothing for the new Canadian companies. That money goes back to the multinationals, the people they purport to dislike. More significantly, what will that cost? We estimate, and the study is here and I will send it over, that that fund will generate about $200 million over the 10-year period.
The opposition parties state that they are following Eastman. I wish to refer them to Dr. Eastman's report, page 365, which deals with this recommendation for the research fund. Dr. Eastman says that in 1983 had that fund been in place there would have been an additional $4.6 million into the research fund. In other words, had that 10 per cent royalty been in place, which the Senate is recommending and the Liberals and the NDP are supporting, that would have generated $4.6 million in research.
In the same paragraph Dr. Eastman states that because that would raise the price of generics by 10 per cent this would induce a price increase in the competing brand name company by an equivalent amount that would result in increased costs to the consumer of between $26.6 million and $30.6 million.
In other words, to generate $4.6 million in research through this fund the consumer has to pay $28.6 million more, about six times as much. Under the scheme the Liberals want, for every $1 million which goes into research the consumer would have to pay $6 million. To generate the $200 million for jobs which the Liberals say will be guaranteed, the consumers will have to put up a mere $1.2 million. What kind of proposal is that? They say they are doing this to help the consumers when what they are proposing will cost consumers $1.2 billion to generate $200 million of research funds.
They say they are doing this on Eastman's recommendation. They have not read Eastman's report. It is on page 365 and is very simple and can be understood. They need not even read the whole page, it is in the first paragraph.
Anyone who claims that they are following what the Senate suggests or recommends in order to protect consumers does not know what they are talking about. Rather than protecting consumers they are hurting them.
The proposal of the Senate will not provide any money for medical faculties. Under Bill C-22, $400 million will go to our teaching hospitals, research institutes, universities and faculties of medicine over the next 10 years. There is nothing in the Senate proposal which the Liberal Party and the New Democrats apparently support which will do that. I repeat that it will do nothing for new companies starting up.
Biomira is a small company in Edmonton run by Dr. Gordon Politeski. They have 30 employees and are developing cancer diagnosis and therapy using synthetic carbohydrate cancer antigens. They are trying to raise some money. They are fairly successful. They have 30 Ph.D. or Masters students and hope

August 21, 1987
Patent Act
to grow to 100. They say that without patent protection their growth will be restricted. If they do develop cancer therapies they are faced with the prospect of having them copied by somebody else.
In Dr. Politeski's notes he says that he is aware of one bright scientist at the University of Alberta who was forced to license a product very early on to a Japanese company because of lack of research dollars. He received $80,000 and the Japanese company recently licensed his product to a U.S. firm for $15 million plus royalties. What a tragedy. What a shocking waste of Canada's intellectual capital. The NDP and Liberals want to carry that on.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Shame, shame!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Why do they not go to the University of Alberta and talk to the scientist involved here, or to Dr. Politeski or anyone involved in this area and see if they can, in all conscience, carry on with this immoral campaign of theirs? There would not be the improved health benefits to Canadians under the Senate amendments which our proposal would produce.
I will relate another anecdote. We have heard arguments about whether this will be real research and whether there will be real benefit to health care. Let me tell you the cardizem story. Cardizem was a drug developed by a Japanese company, a so-called beta blocker to treat hypertension, angina and so on. Through clinical research in Montreal at a company called Nordic it was discovered that cardizem was a calcium blocker. To put that in understandable terms, every year in Canada about 20,000 people will have a heart attack of the so-called inner heart. Of those 10,000, will have a second heart attack within 30 days, and of those, 5,000 will die. Cardizem prevents the second heart attack.
There are literally thousands of people alive today because of this discovery in Montreal. Everybody involved in this says, "You ain't seen nothing yet, you ain't seen what we can do if you pass Bill C-22 and give us the resources to carry on the research we are doing in health care". In the heart area in particular, Montreal is one of the world centres. They have superb capability there. Under this Bill they will get tens of millions of dollars enabling them to hire more of the graduates of our university system and pursue this work and save untold numbers of Canadian lives. Faced with that track record how can anybody in this House vote in conscience without first going to Montreal, talking to those people, and seeing what will be put at risk by pursuing the policy of trying to kill this Bill?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
With regard to manufacturing in Canada, the Bill provides that if you manufacture the fine chemical in Canada, as opposed to importing it from abroad, you can introduce a generic copy after seven years. One manufacturer alone predicts that his company could employ several hundred
people within the next few years if we give him that window of opportunity. None of those jobs are in the 3,000 we have talked about; we have not put those in that category, but there are several hundred jobs in one generic manufacturing company alone that have been put in jeopardy by the amendments from the Senate which the opposition Party apparently wants to support. How can they say that job creation must be a first priority in the country when they will not support this amazing job creation program?
There is the question of cost to consumers. I will repeat again, as I have already done so many times, that 7 per cent of drugs attract a generic competitor. On a value basis it is 20 per cent. That leaves 80 per cent on value or 93 per cent on number of drugs that are monopoly. Right now there is no federal oversight in terms of the price of those drugs. Under our scheme the Drug Prices Review Board will be examining those drugs and keeping the price increases of them at less than the cost of living. If that Board had been in place between 1969 and 1983 there would have been a saving to consumers in Canada of between $80 million and $180 million.
The Opposition dismisses that Board. Dr. Eastman, whose analysis they claim to support, albeit not totally because they have not read his report, will head that Board. He thinks it will be effective. We have policy review by Government and Parliament to ensure that it is effective. We will have annual reports so that parliamentarians can oversee it. In spite of all of that the Opposition and the Senate say it will not work.
How about the savings to provincial Governments in medical research itself? One drug, cimetidine, which goes by the brand name of Tagamet, is an ulcer drug which is fairly expensive. However, it saves net on hospitalization costs each year $130 million because people with peptic ulcers do not have to be hospitalized as frequently as a result of the discovery of that drug. So what if the provinces, through their drug plans, have to spend an extra $50 million on that drug each year if they save $130 million on hospitalization costs? It is a net benefit.
I will now go to the question of this process and whether the Senate has a right to veto the decisions of this House. There is no question that the Constitution and the House of Commons Act say that the Senate has a legal right to kill Bills. It has that right indeed, but I remind Members of the House that the Governor General has the legal right to do the same thing. By refusing to give Royal Assent the Governor General can kill any Bill we pass. However, there is a democratic tradition that the Governor General, as an appointed person, without the mandate of being elected, has no such moral right and the Governor General does not exercise such a moral right and would not do so. If she chose to do so, though I cannot imagine for what reason, there would be a tremendous constitutional crisis in Canada and we might no longer have a Governor General.
August 21, 1987

The Senate threatening to veto this Bill is acting in the same unconstitutional way as in the hypothetical case 1 just mentioned. There is no way that one can morally justify a non-elected body vetoing legislation.
Members of the New Democratic Party say the Senate has no right to exist. If the New Democrats and the Liberals say that the Senate has the right to veto this Bill, then they have to concede that it has the right to veto every Bill. They are saying that, as a Government, we in essence must have Allan MacEachen, the Liberal opposition Leader in the Senate, sitting at the cabinet table.

The people of Canada said that he and the Liberal Government of Pierre Trudeau no longer had a right to sit at a cabinet table deciding what is happening. However, the NDP and the Liberals say that he does, he still has the right to veto this Government's program, he has the right to veto the decisions of this democratically elected House.
1 wonder how the NDP would get by this principle. This is the Party of principle; "We mean what we say and we say what we mean," they say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we cannot have two federal Governments. We cannot have one still led by former Deputy Prime Minister Allan MacEachen overruling the Government in this House. That is a principle that 1 do not think even members of the NDP could support. In fact, that is what they will be doing if they vote in support of what the Senators have done.
I would like to recommend that this House send the following motion back to the other place. 1 move:
That a Message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this House agrees with amendment 10(a) made by the Senate to Bill C-22, An Act to amend the Patent Act and provide for certain matters in relation thereto, but disagrees with all other amendments except amendments 1(c) and 8, because this House believes that amendments 1(a) and (b), 2(a) and (b), 3, 4(a) and (b), 5(a) and (b), 6, 7(a) and (b), 9 and 10(b) and (c) are in contradiction to the principles of the Bill which will increase intellectual
Patent Act
property protection, increase research and development in Canada, create new high-technology jobs, improve the health care of Canadians, and protect consumers from higher drug prices. More specifically:
Amendments 1(a) and (b) delete the definitions of "Board" and "patentee". These definitions are necessary to support the powers of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, which is required to protect consumers.
Amendments 2(a) and (b) reduce Canada's export potential and fine chemical manufacturing.
Amendments 3, 4(a) and (b), reduce the periods of market exclusivity, thus eliminating the incentive for increased research and development in Canada.
Amendment 5(a) reduces the period of market exclusivity and export potential, thus reducing economic benefits for Canada.
Amendment 5(b) deletes the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, which is required to protect consumers, and this amendment also removes the protection for Canadian-invented medicines and thus the incentives for increased research and development in Canada.
Amendments 6, 7(a) and (b), 10(b) and (c) arise out of amendments 1(a) and (b), 2, 3, 4(a) and (b), 5(a) and (b), and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendment 9 arises out of Senate amendment 8, but is not consistent with the House amendment to Senate amendment 8, as set out below.
And, that:
Senate amendment 1(c) be amended to read as follows: "(c) Strike out lines 35 to 42 and add the following:
(2) For the purpose of sections 41.11 to 41.16, the notice of compliance that is first issued for either the original and distinct chemical composition of a medicine or the obvious chemical equivalent of the medicine shall be deemed to be the first notice of compliance issued in respect of that medicine."
Senate amendment 8 be amended to read as follows: "insert the heading "Transitional" and the following as clause 31:
31.(1) The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs shall pay to each province for each of the fiscal years commencing in the period April 1, 1987 to March 31, 1991, for the purpose of research and development relating to medicine, an amount equal to the product obtained by multiplying

Let me give a brief explanation of Amendment 10(a), the amendment we accepted. We had proposed that the Act shall come into force on a day set by proclamation. The Senate amended that to say that the subsections of the Act shall come into force on a day or days as set by proclamation. It provided the Crown with added flexibility. We do not really need it, but if the Senate feels that we should have that added flexibility, we accept that amendment.
We restored the provision for the $100 million to the provinces. I had become increasingly convinced based on

August 21, 1987

However, a commitment of $100 million had been made. We will honour that commitment, but 1 would hope everyone in the House would agree that that money ought to go to medical research. We are paying the money to the provinces for medical research, it will be theirs to administers to the research communities in the way they see fit and we hope that that is in keeping with Parliament's commitment to research and development.
The other Senate amendment which we amended further had to do with the 10-year period of exclusivity. It was a case of two sets of lawyers disagreeing. The lawyer the Senate had hired felt that our definition was not precise. The lawyers in the Justice Department advised us that it was. We have come up with new wording which will hopefully satisfy the Justice lawyers as well as Mr. French, the lawyer the Senators hired for $800 a day.
That is the gist of the motion. I recommend it to the House. 1 have copies of the amendment. 1 will put them on the Table and make them available for anyone who would like to see them.
I humbly ask all Hon. Members to consider what is at stake, which is, Canada's reputation, jobs, research and development and Canada's health care system. I hope all Hon. subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF HITLER-STALIN PACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Sunday, August 23, is Black Ribbon Day, the anniversary of the
signing of the Hitler-Stalin Friendship and Non-Agression Pact in 1939. That treaty divided Poland between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, authorized the U.S.S.R. to take over Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania, and signalled the beginning of World War II just 10 days later.
On Sunday, the International Black Ribbon Day Committee in Toronto, together with similar committees across Canada, Britain, Australia, Sweden, France and the United States will hold rallies to remember the partition of Europe, honour the millions of people who lost their freedom behind the Iron Curtain, and give thanks for our own freedom.
All those who cherish peace with freedom should join with the International Black Ribbon Day Committee this Sunday as they call on the Soviet Union to live up to its repeated statements in support of peace and detente by renouncing the Nazi-Soviet Friendship Pact, something it has never done, and by honouring its Yalta commitment to allow free democratic elections in eastern Europe.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) concluded his remarks concerning certain Senate amendments to Bill C-22. Over the course of about 30 or 40 minutes he accused the Senate of being undemocratic and made a number of other disparaging comments. Having said all that, he then proceeded to accept a number of those amendments. One could conclude that the Minister was being somewhat hypocritical. First he says the Senate is undemocratic and useless and should not be amending House of Commons legislation. Then in the same breath he accepts certain of those amendments. That would lead one to conclude that the legislation was faulty and in need of amendment.
Not only that, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) also accepted Senate amendments to certain pieces of his legislation. Canadians can see through both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. This legislation is not in the best interests of Canadian consumers.

subtopic: FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-DECLINE IN SHARE OF MARKET
FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-DECLINE IN SHARE OF MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Government dropped most quotas on imported footwear some 21 months ago, it predicted the shoe industry in Canada would thrive despite the change. Instead, as we predicted, and as The Financial Post reported this week, the change in policy "has dealt a crushing blow to much of the Canadian shoe industry".
The market share of Canadian producers has fallen from 41 per cent in December, 1985, to 35 per cent in December, 1986. The Shoe Manufacturers Association says the decline is continuing. Jobs in the industry have fallen by 11 per cent. For many small communities across Ontario and Quebec, the cost has been tragic. This shows what the Government's free trade, market-oriented ideas will create elsewhere in the economy.
The Government's strategy for the shoe industry has been to give up and retreat, instead of carrying through the restructuring process which we would have supported and which would have meant a modern effective future for this industry.

speechtext:

subtopic: OPENING OF WORLD'S LARGEST OPEN PIT GOLD MINE AT HEDLEY, B.C.
OPENING OF WORLD'S LARGEST OPEN PIT GOLD MINE AT HEDLEY, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the OECD reports that economic growth in Canada in 1986 was the strongest among the major industrialized countries. Today I report more good news for Canadians.
On Monday I attended the official opening of the world's largest open pit gold mine at Hedley in the riding 1 represent. The $61 million investment in the Mascot Gold Mine creates hundreds of jobs for Canadians and demonstrates the new private sector confidence generated by the policies and actions of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) Government. Socialist policies promoted by the NDP and their Liberal cousins are designed to discourage private sector activity, leaving everything up to big government. Mr. Speaker, there is one group of victims of Canada's recession of the 1980s who have not recovered and whom the Government is ignoring. I am speaking of the growing group of older workers who have been without work for more than a year. Last year these people made up 7.7 per cent of the unemployed. This year they make up 9.3 per cent.
The Labour Adjustment Benefits Program is discontinued and the program of adjustment for older workers has not started.
It is not good enough for the Government to blame the provinces. The Conservatives ended the only program helping older workers. It is time for them to deliver on their promise to create a new one.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GERALDINE KENNEY-WALLACE TO HEAD SCIENCE COUNCIL OF CANADA
APPOINTMENT OF GERALDINE KENNEY-WALLACE TO HEAD SCIENCE COUNCIL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced this morning the appointment of Dr. Geraldine Kenney-Wallace as chairperson of the Science Council of Canada.
Dr. Kenney-Wallace is Professor of Chemistry and Physics, and Chairman of the Research Board at the University of Toronto. She is an international authority on lasers and nonlinear optics.
Educated at the Royal Institute in London, and the University of British Columbia, she is the author of over 80 research papers. She is currently a member of the Science Council and of the Premier of Ontario's Advisory Council on Technology.
She has held Sloan Foundation, Guggenheim, and Steacie research fellowships, and Noranda and Sigma XI lectureships.
In addition to her impressive academic credentials, she has a special talent for promoting public awareness of the importance of science and technology. She is an eloquent spokesperson on the role of science and technology in the lives of contemporary Canadians.
She is an important addition to the science and technology team that this Government is putting together. I, as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology, join with others in the House in welcoming her to her new responsibilities.

subsubtopic: CODE OF CONDUCT-INTRODUCTION OF REFORM PACKAGE
speechtext: In the absence of the Prime Minister, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. The Acting Prime Minister will know that many months ago the Government promised to introduce a package of reforms concerning conflict of interest, the tendering process, and the financing of political Parties. The people of Canada are still waiting. It has been more than seven months since this promise was made. Will the Acting Prime Minister assure the House that we will have this package of reforms introduced in time to be put in place before the next election?

under very active consideration and action has been taken with respect to lobbyists. subsubtopic: INDIVIDUALS AND FINANCING
speechtext: This is a priority for Canadians. More specifically, with respect to the financing of political parties, is the Minister prepared to guarantee that the Government will table a Bill that would allow only private individuals to make donations to political parties?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INDIVIDUALS AND FINANCING
speechtext:

Members will have a chance to review this legislation so that we can bring it forward very soon.

subsubtopic: PARKER INQUIRY REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns the report of the Parker Inquiry into the conflict of interest allegations against the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. The Deputy Prime Minister indicated that the Government might be looking to that particular report with regard to new rules and regulations with respect to conflict of interest.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister with some degree of precision indicate to the House when that report might be made public and tabled in the House of Commons? Can he also indicate what the total cost of the inquiry will be? We know that the legal fees for the former Minister to the tune of about $650,000 have been paid. I am sure that Canadians would like to know what the total cost of this particular inquiry will be.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF FORMER MINISTER'S LEGAL FEES
PAYMENT OF FORMER MINISTER'S LEGAL FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister answered only one part of my question. He did not answer the other part. I am sure that the Government does have some answers with regard to the total cost of the Parker Inquiry.
Canadians are outraged that the Government of Canada decided to pay the legal fees of the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. I have a letter from the Department indicating the reasons why the Minister's legal fees were paid. The letter states that the payment is being
August 21, 1987

made "on the basis that the Commission is investigating the conduct of Mr. Stevens as a Minister" and therefore lies within established precedents. We all know that the inquiry was looking into the personal conduct of the Minister and that that excuse is a flimsy rationale for paying the legal fees of that particular Minister. subsubtopic: BILL C-22-COST OF RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The pharmaceutical companies will be given a 10-year monopoly lay Bill C-22 when it becomes law on the basis of a promise that they will spend about $1.4 billion in additional money. Some 60 per cent of that additional research expenditure, however, will be written off at a cost to Canadian taxpayers.
Will the Minister confirm that, given this 60 per cent writeoff and the increased prices of patented pharmaceuticals, in effect the taxpayers will be paying for substantially all of that research?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL C-22-COST OF RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada, along with I think every other industrialized nation, provides that research and development is deductible for tax purposes. In fact most nations have more generous incentives. So one can say that, if one uses the logic that all money belongs to the Government first and foremost and any deduction from income therefore is a contribution from the Government to that effort, then on that basis the Government makes that contribution to research and development, whether it is in the field of pharmaceuticals, widgets, mousetraps or what-have-you.
Is it the position of the NDP that in fact research and development ought not to be tax deductible? If that position were implemented, then the small amount of research being conducted in Canada would turn out to be zero. I am sure the
Oral Questions
Hon. Member would want to think that out before he adopts it as his Party's position.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows that drug profits are among the highest in manufacturing, with a 20 per cent average in 1985, and some as high as 50 per cent, transfer pricing, and now a 10-year monopoly. After years of profitable business in Canada how does the Minister justify this raping of the Canadian taxpayer for a group which, before 1969, would not do research and cannot be expected without firm commitments to do so now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member does his sums I know that he has based them on a newspaper article this morning written by Dan Westell. What was incomplete in that study was that it did not look at the additional tax revenue from those 3,000 scientists being employed in Canada rather than overseas, the scientific people, and so on, in the high-tech jobs. Those are the spinout benefits of that. If the Hon. Member wants to do a tax balance on that he should consider all the factors.
As I pointed out many times in committee, a company that does not do research does not deduct that from its income. If in 1983 the companies had been spending 10 per cent of revenue on research as opposed to 5 per cent, then their return on investment would have been a normal industrial return. They show a higher return because they are taking that money out of Canada. We want it spent here in research and development which, incidentally, has the effect of reducing their income after taxes.

subsubtopic: INDUSTRY'S SITUATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The shipbuilding industry in Atlantic Canada has been asking the federal Government for assistance. Not only has it been denied this assistance but the Minister of Public Works has said that the shipbuilding industry should take a long, hard look at itself and perhaps pick a shipyard in the region that could close its doors forever.
This is a treacherous response to an industry that needs help badly and one that has been led to believe that help would be forthcoming from the Government. Why does the Government not take a long, hard look at itself and realize that its failure to keep its commitment is sabotaging the shipbuilding industry in Atlantic Canada?

subsubtopic: INDUSTRY'S SITUATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

August 21, 1987
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: INDUSTRY'S SITUATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too share the concern of the Hon. Member. 1 think he would also agree with the fact that there is some 60 per cent of over-capacity in the shipbuilding industry throughout the world, which has had a major effect in depressing prices in the industry. The Government has responded by providing a tremendous amount of work to the shipbuilding industry. Something in the order of 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the business done in the shipbuilding industry is provided by government contracts.
There has been some degree of rationalization in the Canadian shipbuilding industry. That has taken place throughout the world. It is simply in concert with the realities of the international situation. I can assure the Hon. Member that we will, as a Government, work with the industry in trying to pursue the course of rationalization in a manner which would not provoke undue dislocation.

Mr. Speaker, during the 1984 election campaign the Government dangled over the heads of the people in Atlantic Canada that it was going to provide $75 million to develop shipbuilding in Canadian ports. Atlantic Canada has not received the benefit of that promise.
Why will the Government not keep its promise, create these jobs in shipyards in Atlantic Canada, and create the needed employment that has been looked forward to in Atlantic Canada as a result of the promises of the Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member in his good intentions might wish to prevail upon his Leader and his critic for defence matters, and persuade them to support the initiatives of the Government in terms of the White Paper in which the Government is calling for the building of a number of nuclear submarines.
This would provide some 55,000 person years of work. That is the manner in which the Hon. Member can help. Those jobs would be created in Canada for the shipbuilding industry. I urge that the Hon. Member raise that issue with his caucus and his Leader.

subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF ALLEGED WAR CRIMINALS TO CANADA-ROLE OF FORMER RCMPOFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General.
In a recent study by Alti Rodal it was revealed that in 1983 a senior RCMP officer and member of the security service deliberately ignored federal policy and destroyed records to facilitate the entry into Canada of two alleged Nazi war criminals, one of whom was a member of the SS.
Will the Solicitor General confirm that this is accurate? Will he indicate whether or not this individual is currently a member of CSIS? If these allegations are in fact accurate, and this person lied to his political masters and destroyed documents, will the Minister not accept his responsibility and ensure that this person is fired from CSIS for these reprehensible actions?

subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF ALLEGED WAR CRIMINALS TO CANADA-ROLE OF FORMER RCMPOFFICER
speechtext: Who was the Solicitor General at the time?

subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF ALLEGED WAR CRIMINALS TO CANADA-ROLE OF FORMER RCMPOFFICER

Mr. Speaker, I can advise the Hon. Member that this incident occurred in 1983. The person was a member of the RCMP at that time, and an administrative decision was made to move him out of the area that dealt with immigration and screening, or anything to do with the area of citizenship.
I am advised that today he still does remain a member of CSIS, who transferred from the RCMP to CSIS. He is employed in an area that has absolutely nothing to do with immigration or citizenship matters.

subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF ALLEGED WAR CRIMINALS TO CANADA-ROLE OF FORMER RCMPOFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely shocking that a member who was responsible for lying and destroying federal documents has not been disciplined whatsoever, but has merely been moved from one section to another.

subsubtopic: OECD REPORT-UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:

The Prime Minister did not quote statements in the report that Canada's unemployment rate is "high by historical standards, and compared to the OECD average", and "is likely to remain above its pre-recession level". This, Mr. Speaker, in the fifth year of recovery.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House if the Government really is satisfied with its record over the past three years, as the Prime Minister indicated yesterday?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subsubtopic: NATIONAL SALES TAX PROPOSAL
speechtext:
My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The OECD report quoted yesterday also noted "a sharp decline in disposable income". It stated that Canada's higher than average inflation rate was due, in large part, to "indirect tax increases".
Since the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and other groups, are also calling for up-front visible taxes, is the Minister now prepared to be open with Canadians and reveal the hidden part of his tax strategy, which is the national sales tax?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL SALES TAX PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will make his statements on

national sales tax in due course. It is not for me to announce that on his behalf.

subsubtopic: WHITE WATER RAFTING FATALITIES-STRICTER REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport, or in his absence to the Parliamentary Secretary to that Minister.
This year 12 persons have died in four separate river-rafting accidents in British Columbia. It seems imperative that the Department of Transport amend the Boating Restriction Regulations which are in place in British Columbia in order that permits for commercial river-rafting operations be required on all waters in that province.
What action has been taken in response to these tragic accidents to bring an element of regulated safety into the business of river rafting in British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: WHITE WATER RAFTING FATALITIES-STRICTER REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen for his question.
The Government has acted in this area. Indeed, the Boating Restriction Regulations were declared on August 14, and will be published in The Canada Gazette on September 2.
We also have agreement with the provincial Government of British Columbia to change the river-rafting standards. It is regrettable that again government has to move in because people do not use some sense of their own. The Government has acted.

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES OF RISKY BANK LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. Can the Minister confirm that the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce received the approval of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the Government to transfer about $850 million to its reserves against high-risk foreign loans, that this transfer will reduce taxes payable by the CIBC by about

August 21, 1987
Oral Questions
$400 million and that consequently, the Bank will probably not pay any income tax at all for the current financial year? Does the situation really warrant the Government's approving this change in the Bank's accounts that will mean the CIBC will not have to pay any income tax for the current financial year?

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES OF RISKY BANK LOANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the tax provisions and the loss provisions that will be taken as a result of this loan experience mean the following for that bank: under current tax practice and consistent with tax reform, it will be taking its losses this year. If its experience should improve over time from what it projects, when the income comes into revenue it will be taxable. That is quite different from outright forgiveness which the Hon. Member's Party has often suggested. Under outright forgiveness there is a massive deduction. Banks will not pay taxes for many years under outright forgiveness, plus it is irreversible.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister confirms that there will be a very substantial writeoff, which will, in fact, cut $400 million from the tax liability of the Bank of Commerce for the fiscal year 1987 and probably result in it paying no tax at all on its profits despite substantial profits on domestic business in 1987.
Does the Minister not agree that it is about time that we had a minimum tax on corporations, including the banks, so that they could write something like this off over a number of years, as was the previous practice, rather than forcing the taxpayers to pay all of these losses in one year?

Mr. Speaker, I fail to see the accounting significance of what the Member is suggesting. Whether the banks take the write-off this year or over time, the effect in terms of tax revenues is virtually the same.

subsubtopic: MEECH LAKE ACCORD-EQUALITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I will direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday I asked the Prime Minister to dissociate himself and his Government from the suggestion that women's groups are opposing the Meech Lake distinct society clause because they do not want Quebec to be recognized as having a distinct society.
In reply yesterday, right here in the House, the Prime Minister once again expressed approval of the newspaper column by Lysiane Gagnon in which that view was strongly
expressed. However, in front of the committee yesterday the Government's own Advisory Council on the Status of Women expressed concern about the equality rights provisions in the Meech Lake Accord.
Will the Government simply recognize the good faith of that point of view?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEECH LAKE ACCORD-EQUALITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond to that question again today because we want this matter to be put in the proper perspective. It was determined by the First Ministers that if there was an egregious error made with respect to the provisions of the Meech Lake Accord consideration would naturally be given to amendments to rectify that error.
Fortunately, there has been no indication to the present time, on the basis of our best legal advice, that there is such an error with respect to the rights of women or any other group in Canada, including minority groups. The best legal advice that we have, which is supported by very eminent authorities, is that women's rights in particular are in fact unaffected in a negative manner by the Accord.
As the Hon. Member knows, because he is participating, we have a committee which is doing very good work in examining all facets of this matter and hearing from well respected groups and organizations.
I thought the Prime Minister answered the Member's question very well yesterday in that he cast no aspersions with respect to motivation on the part of any women's group which has appeared before the committee. That is the situation and it should be accepted by the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice has just told us that it was determined by the First Ministers that only egregious errors would be recognized and corrected. Whose Constitution is this? It is not the First Ministers' Constitution but the Constitution of Canada.
Various groups of Canadians are coming forward to express their views about the Constitution. Are they not entitled to try to improve the Meech Lake Accord, egregious errors or not? Are they not entitled to have a say? Are the views which are coming forward with so much support and so much good sense not worth considering?
To put it in one question, why will the Government not recognize that the Meech Lake Accord, as good as it is and as important as it is, is capable of being made better?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not this Government which gave the country its process for amending the Constitution. It was the Government of which the Hon. Member was a part which set the process in place with respect to the amendment of our Constitution.
August 21, 1987

I think this particular amendment is a historic point in our history which should be supported wholeheartedly by all Canadians. The entry of Quebec into the Constitution is something which we as Canadians should applaud and support.
We naturally want to consider improving our Constitution. Indeed, one of the most important elements in terms of the agreement reached by the First Ministers was the provision that henceforth we will have an annual constitutional meeting among First Ministers at which improvements to our Constitution can be examined. This has never been the case before. The Government is giving more consideration to the sensitivities of our country than has any previous administration.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Minister.

subsubtopic: PIANO FACTORY-PROTECTION RECOMMENDED BY TARIFF REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last piano factory in this country in Clinton, Ontario, is facing closure because of competition from Korea. It took its case to the Tariff Review Board, won that case, and the Board recommended extra protection to the Government.
I would like to direct my question to the Minister of State for Finance. Why has the Government not yet moved to implement these recommendations in order to protect these jobs that matter so much to the small community of Clinton, Ontario?

subsubtopic: PIANO FACTORY-PROTECTION RECOMMENDED BY TARIFF REVIEW BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for raising this issue. I hope to be meeting with the management of the company in Clinton in the next week to discuss this matter. There are problems with the business plan which concern the viability of this firm as well as tariff questions which have to be discussed.

Mr. Speaker, could the Minister also explain why a meeting which was set up with the Minister of Finance and this company was cancelled? Why has the Government rejected loan guarantees for this factory despite firm export orders which the company has for 1,200 piano sales to the United States? In short, why is the Government ignoring this small community's future?

Mr. Speaker, we know that loan guarantees can be given when we know that a firm can be viable in the short term, medium term and long run. That is what we are trying to assess. Hopefully that will be done in the next week to 10 days.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS-METRO TORONTO SPEED LIMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport I will direct my question to the Parliamentary Secretary. On July 14 last a CP train carrying hazardous materials and travelling at a speed of about 40 miles per hour derailed in my constituency. Fortunately, the car that contained the hazardous materials did not derail.
One year ago, at the request of the former Minister of Transport, the present Deputy Prime Minister, CP Rail voluntarily imposed a 25 mile per hour speed limit on trains carrying dangerous goods on a portion of their track in Metro Toronto. Unfortunately, the derailment this time occurred on another portion of track where that limit was not imposed.
Will the Parliamentary Secretary give us his undertaking today that he and the Minister will immediately request CP Rail to impose a 25 mile per hour speed limit for all of their trains carrying hazardous goods through Metropolitan Toronto? If they refuse to do so, will he instruct the CTC to institute a mandatory speed limit of 25 miles per hour in this area?

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS-METRO TORONTO SPEED LIMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that we never tire of the questions of the Hon. Member for York East and on this one he has certainly been persistent. The Minister is vitally concerned about this as, indeed, are all Members of Parliament.
As the Member knows, there is a task force studying the whole question of Toronto and the routes of tracks through the Metropolitan area, due to its explosive growth. I believe that task force is to report in March of 1988.
However, in the meantime I will, of course, consult with the Minister on this. I am sure the Minister will speak with CP because it may well be appropriate for that 25 mile per hour zone to be extended to cover the area within the Member's riding. We will certainly take that up and give it serious consideration.

subsubtopic: MOZAMBIQUE-REQUEST FOR MORE ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, my question is addressed to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Deputy Prime Minister knows only too well that front-line states in southern Africa are indeed on the front line and that in fact Mozambique in particular is being terrorized

August 21, 1987
Oral Questions
and has had its transportation and infrastructures destroyed by the South African forces. In fact, the Red Cross has made an appeal about that and has borne eloquent testimony to it.
Is Canada prepared to match its rhetoric beyond its emergency food aid and some $24 million from CIDA? Is it prepared to take some meaningful steps to bolster the economy of Mozambique which unfortunately receives one of the lowest percentages and rates of assistance from Canada's aid program?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOZAMBIQUE-REQUEST FOR MORE ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the Secretary of State for External Affairs just returned from a visit to that region of the world. I would certainly undertake to raise the Hon. Member's question with him. I think he will be in the House next week and I am sure that he would be only too happy to respond in a definitive way.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CO-ORDINATED MEASURES TO AID AFRICAN FRONT-LINE STATES
REQUEST FOR CO-ORDINATED MEASURES TO AID AFRICAN FRONT-LINE STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while this tragedy in Mozambique is unfolding, Canada is not putting its money and its efforts where its mouth is and its visitors are. Does Canada have any firm, specific, concrete proposals to make before the Francophone Conference and the Commonwealth Conference for an organized, coordinated effort to get emergency medium and long-range aid, grants and expertise to these front-line states? Does it have any proposals for strengthening and diversifying their economies so that they do not have to depend on trade with South Africa?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CO-ORDINATED MEASURES TO AID AFRICAN FRONT-LINE STATES
speechtext:
