subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate. However, I am disappointed that the Minister of the Crown supporting this Bill is probably unavoidably-

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Just outside in the lobby.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
He will be back? I accept the word of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski).
It is interesting to note that for a number of days we have had comments by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and of course the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) concerning the process that Bill C-22, amendments to the Patent Act, is presently undergoing. We have heard time and time again sentiments expressed by government Members which seem to be very consistent. Yet as time goes on we find their statements are not backed up by their actions. I believe the Minister has swallowed himself on Bill C-22. I believe the Prime Minister has also swallowed himself over the process involving Bill C-22.
For your listening pleasure, and for the record, I want to read what the Prime Minister of Canada has said about the legality and constitutionality of the Upper Chamber and its debate over Bill C-22. I quote:
This is being choked off by a handful of non-elected Liberal Senators who are in turn in the process of inflicting very serious and perhaps irreparable damage to the scientific well-being of Quebec. This Act by an unelected, undemocratic group shall be resisted by every Quebecer, by every elected Member of Parliament irrespective of the side of the House he or she happens to be on. 1 tell you, there will not be a Liberal left or an NDPer left if this is the attitude they propose to display to the people of Canada.
Those were the words of the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada regarding the legality and constitutionality of the Senate in its debate on Bill C-22.
Logically one would automatically assume that any amendments coming from the Senate would not be accepted by the Minister. That is what he has said repeatedly on the electronic media. Yet some of those amendments have been agreed to by the Government. If there was ever an example of hypocrisy, of swallowing oneself, it has to be the behaviour of the Minister concerned and of course the Prime Minister.
To say for the last number of days that no changes by an unelected bunch of political hacks will be accepted and to then turn around and do the exact opposite, as has been done on previous occasions on other Bills, indicates to me quite clearly that the Government is trying to have it both ways. It wants to be in a position to criticize the Senate when it is to its advantage. Yet when the Canadian people cry out, as they have regarding these amendments to the Patent Act through a number of representations to the committee examining Bill C-22, you can see that the Government of the Right Hon. Prime Minister wishes to disassociate itself from such political hacks as Michel Cogger, Jean Bazin, Finlay MacDonald, Lowell Murray, and a number of other individuals. That is what the Government wishes to do.
I suggest, to be fair and reasonable, that the Conservative Government cannot have it both ways. It either believes in the legal and constitutional authority of the Upper Chamber or it does not. If it continues this kind of inflamed rhetoric, then the Prime Minister and the Minister should have the common
August 21, 1987

decency to place before this Chamber legislation to reform the Upper Chamber.
We know the Prime Minister speaks with a forked-tongue. He says one thing and does the opposite. There are numerous examples of that. This is another undisputed example of the Prime Minister of Canada, aided and abetted by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who accepted some of the Senate amendments, contradicting themselves and practising another degree of hypocrisy.
There is such a thing in this country as a Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It has been said by others that this is a Minister of corporate affairs, not one who, while perhaps legally authorized to do so, stands up to protect and enhance the rights of consumers. He is a Minister who is intrigued by corporate affairs and the web of connections in the corporate world. He is mystified by the international glamour of multinational corporations. Earlier today we saw the display of a Minister of corporate affairs who is concerned about protecting and enhancing the multinational fabric in the international world.
We heard a Minister of corporate affairs take another giant step in an attempt to perpetrate on Canadians his wisdom or expertise with regard to the constitutionality of a second chamber. The result was a clear, unequivocal message to Canadians that although he is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), his mandate has but one objective, to serve the masters of the corporate world.
His predecessors in previous Governments as well as his own saw their mandate as one to enhance and improve the rights and privileges of the Canadian consumer. This morning, we saw a despicable display by a Minister of the Crown. I say to him that he and his Government will pay the price for legislation that is fundamentally flawed. There were suggestions in the committee and in both Houses, as well as by individuals across the country, of ways and means to improve the Bill. However, the Minister has chosen to protect and enhance the multinational corporations.
1 am sorry to say that I must hold the Minister responsible to those thousands of Canadians who want reasonable and affordable drugs, who want jobs in this country and want research and development. They want to see a Canadian pharmaceutical industry but we have seen the complete opposite from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I believe a Bill should be introduced to change the name of his portfolio to corporate and international affairs, to advance the right of Pfizer in the United States which had profits last year in excess of $600 million.
While there is nothing wrong with the profit motive, we are not in the business as legislators of seeing to one aspect of this industry, namely, profitability. We have signed an oath to represent the best interests of all Canadians and thereby try to
Patent Act
establish a public policy that addresses the fundamental pillars of a pharmaceutical society.
Let me say to the Minister that some of the things he has said in this chamber are partly correct but, as usual, he has chosen his words carefully in order to portray, as inaccurate as it is, an image of what members of this Party are attempting to do with regard to Bill C-22. It was the New Democratic Party that wanted no changes to the 1969 Act on pharmaceuticals. It is the Tories and the Minister of corporate affairs who want to give more to the multinationals. Consistently, since the hearing process began in the House of Commons, throughout Question Period, through the debate, and even in the Senate, we have adopted a reasonable set of proposals predicated upon the recommendations of Doctor Eastman, an authority recognized by all Members of Parliament and all political parties. We have attempted to put reasonable proposals to the Government through the committee hearings. There were 48 amendments in the House of Commons which the Conservatives defeated. Now they want to do away with the amendments that members in the other House have taken upon themselves to return to us in the House of Commons.
I find it peculiar, if not somewhat extraordinarily unusual, that the Government would go to such great lengths in attempting to perpetrate a lie to the Canadian people. We have indicated what changes we want to the legislation. They are reasonable amendments, keeping in mind that we are a Party which is concerned about the well-being of Canadians and the prices they will have to pay for drugs. We are concerned about having more research and development take place in this country, certainly in Montreal and Quebec. We want to see jobs created. However, our Party and other witnesses have told the Minister time and time again that he is not heading in the right direction. He is only responding to one element of the process. It takes more than multinational corporations to develop a Canadian pharmaceutical industry. A Canadian pharmaceutical industry means multinational corporations operating here in Canada, as well as generic companies operating in Canada. It means the protection of consumers and more research and development that is not only conducted by multinationals.
Again, the Minister of corporate affairs has attempted to perpetrate another lie, that the generic companies are the only group we want doing research and development in Canada. We want the multinational corporations as well as the generic companies to do more research and development in this country, whether it be clinical research, basic research, innovative research, or a combination of those. That is our desire. But when one examines the Bill it becomes more clear that those objectives cannot and will not be met by that legislation. So you see, Mr. Speaker, there is a difference between the governing Party and our Party. There is also a major difference and distinction between our Party and the New Democratic Party with regard to the Patent Act.

August 21, 1987
Patent Act
The Minister of Corporate Affairs-I have now by virtue of an Order in Council in my caucus changed the name of his particular portfolio-has tried to share some thoughts with Canadians on the floor of the House of Commons. He would lead us to believe that on the issue of intellectual property rights, somehow we in Canada are the target of abuse by other foreign countries with regard to intellectual property rights affecting the pharmaceuticals. Let us look at that one realistically.
The raison d'Etat of a multinational corporation is what? The raison d'Etat of a multinational corporation is profit. There is nothing wrong with that. That is their mode of operation. It is profit, profit, profit and profit. Let us look not at figures that I, as an opposition Member of Parliament, would want to put on the floor of the House of Commons for debate, but let us look at the figures which are being given by a distinguished authority in the person of Dr. Eastman. Dr. Eastman submitted a report. From 1969 to 1983 under the old law-not Bill C-22-were the profits reasonable for these multinational corporations? Perhaps they were keeping in line with the manufacturing sector. The answer is that the most profitable sector in manufacturing was the pharmaceutical industry. It made unprecedented profits. The average employment in the manufacturing sector for that period was 4 per cent. In the pharmaceutical industry it was 29 per cent. That is not bad. It is a very profitable industry. The law said that if one invents a pharmaceutical drug in Canada, one must pay.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says "if' and then leaves the Chamber. I know he will be back. He will want to participate in the debate because he feels as strongly about it as I do.
If you are to use that particular drug that was invented by an individual, you had to pay a 4 per cent royalty. That is the system. That is how it works. The industry is profitable. Its profits are way up. Employment is up. It receives a 4 per cent royalty from those individuals who wish to reproduce its particular drug. That is not a very bad situation to be in. The Tories now say that over and above that we have to give the pharmaceutical industry a 10 year period of exclusivity; not a month, not two months, not three months, but 10 years. That is not so the industry will be just a little more profitable, but that it will be much, much more profitable.
In turn, these multinational corporations with headquarters in Switzerland and the United States are going to promise- not give us a consummated contract-that for all that money we have given them, besides the new additional 10 year period of exclusivity over the next 10 years, they will do some research and development. There is no written contract, no guarantee, none whatsoever.
It is the poorer people of my province, in my constituency, the poorer people in Manitoba and Newfoundland, the senior citizens in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario and
Quebec, the farmers of western Canada, the shipbuilding yard worker in British Columbia, the good people of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, who will now have to pay higher drug prices to profitable multinational corporations which will then become more profitable and which then will have a 10 year period of exclusivity, over and above, on the promise that maybe-but maybe not-they will do research and development.
In some parts of my constituency I know what the people would call that. The first four letters spell "bull". I am not going to say the last word because it may be unparliamentary, but that, too, is a four-letter word.
I would think that those of us who have the privilege of sitting in Parliament, of taking an oath to serve the best interests of the Canadian people, would look at such a situation and say, "Surely to God we would want to have as a bare minimum some guarantees of jobs, some guarantees of keeping the prices down and some guarantees of research and development". But what do we have? We have the multinational corporations getting richer and the Canadian people getting poorer as a result of this legislation.
I told you, Mr. Speaker, what is the policy of the New Democratic Party. It wants no amendments, no changes. The Tories want a period of 10 years exclusivity. I have said to the Deputy Prime Minister, as he knows, and I have said it in committee, that we favour a four-year period of exclusivity. We favour having the multinational corporations, as well as Canadian companies, (jay a certain amount into a royalty fund for the purposes of research and development.
I even said to the Minister to keep an open mind. If he finds that the royalty fund I am suggesting is not in keeping with what he believes would achieve the objective he is trying to achieve, let us try to work something out to address that, but let us have some guarantees for jobs, guarantees in terms of the distribution of that wealth, because I know the good people of Alberta, like the good people of Nova Scotia, are getting sick and tired of the benefits of national public policy accruing to certain specific areas of this country.
With certain public will, and political will, I might add, we can change that sentiment and perception felt by the various regions of the country. The Government has chosen repeatedly and consistently to refuse that type of suggestion. I am dismayed.
When I entered Parliament I thought we were here to try to develop good public policy, to address the fundamentals of that particular sector. I thought we were here to try to improve the lot of all Canadians, and not just Pfizer of New York City whose profits in the first quarter of this year were in excess of $600 million.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
How about in Canada?
August 21, 1987

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
1 find the conduct and the behaviour of government Members to be despicable in view of the facts. The facts are there for all of us to examine and to read.
1 would now like to return to the argument of the intellectual property right. Canada is the envy of the world when it comes to pharmaceuticals. I was down in Washington one month ago and I met with a Congressman by the name of Henry Waxman who heads up a subcommittee which looks into the pricing of pharmaceuticals in the United States. I met with Mr. Bill Haddad who was the chairman of the generic industry in the United States. They acclaimed Canada as having the greatest system. There are those in the United States who would like to adopt or at least examine more fully the prospect of adopting such a system in the United States.
I do not want to suggest to my good friend the Deputy Prime Minister that there is a pending law which is similar to the one in Canada-there is not. However, there is a movement, a serious movement to have put in place the type of law that we now have before us, inclusive of the amendments thereto. Consumer groups in the United States have acknowledged the tremendous piece of legislative work done back in 1969 which met the objectives of the Government of the day. Of all the Members of Parliament at that time, did the Conservative Party of the day vote against the Bill? No, it did not.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Who was the Prime Minister?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I believe the Prime Minister at that time was the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, if my memory serves me well, one of the greats, as my hon. friend from New Brunswick across the way acknowledges. Perhaps he is the greatest the Hon. Member says. I would agree with that, he is the greatest. The Conservative Party did not vote against the Bill at that time. Surely, it must have examined and decided at that point in time that that piece of legislation would not contravene any international legislation. Members opposite would lead one to believe that the present legislation, with the amendments of the Liberal Party, would somehow be in contravention of international convention.
A gentleman by the name of Roy Davidson, who was educated at the Universities of Alberta and Toronto, and who for many years was a senior administrator of the bureau of competition policy, and who for some time was the senior economic advisor in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, said the following. I think his words are worth noting, particularly in view of what the Government has been saying. He stated: "Compulsory licensing provisions of the Patent Act are not in contravention of the International Patent Convention of 1904". So when we hear the present Minister, whose title was changed as of 20 minutes ago to the Minister of corporate affairs, say that Canada is not in sync with what is happening internationally, he is wrong.
Patent Act
I asked the Minister in committee where the documented evidence is that says that we are in contravention of international law. There is no evidence, none whatsoever. It is an argument put forward by a weak Government which is bent on serving its political masters, namely, the multinational corporate sector that exists in Canada and throughout the world, and not the Canadian consumers.
After I heard the present Minister of corporate affairs say in the House that we are in contravention of the Bill of Rights I went to my law books. You know, Mr. Speaker, perhaps as Canada's most distinguished legal body-and I think that ought to be underlined in Hansard-that with regard to that argument, the Federal Court has said that Canada is not contravening international conventions with its compulsory licensing, not the Patent Act or the Bill of Rights. Let us not have any more of these falsehoods. Let us not have any more of these inaccurate, grandiose, 30-second clips by the Minister of corporate affairs, because that is not true at all.
That is the first point I want to make with regard to intellectual property rights. Let there be no mistake about it, Canada is not in breach of the International Patent Convention of 1904. Nor is it in breach of the Bill of Rights. As I found out from legal counsel in committee after questioning them extensively, it is not in contravention of GATT, not one iota. There is good law on the books now. I know that my colleagues to the left, the real left, would want me to make this point on their behalf. It is a spurious, fake, false argument to try to perpetrate against the Canadian people with regard to the law with which we are now dealing.
I was in Washington and spoke with legal counsel for Mr. Waxman who chairs that subcommittee. I spoke with Republican staffers as well as to Senators and Congressman. I was struck by the high cost of prescription drugs in the United States. They are phenomenal, absolutely phenomenal.
The law put forward in 1969 by a Liberal administration, and supported by the New Democratic Party, and the Conservative Party, has been working reasonably well for Canadians. It struck me even more I listened to the consumer advocate groups in the United States ask why the Canadian Government is now changing its laws to something similar to those in the United States? Does the Government not realize that consumers in the United States are paying phenomenal drug costs? Is that what the Government wants to do in Canada? I wanted to give an answer which would have supported my Government. But I believe that the evidence available, which has been submitted to committee, allows each reasonable individual to come to the conclusion that we will pay higher drug prices in Canada as a result of the Conservatives pushing through this Bill amending the Patent Act regarding the pharmaceuticals.
Canadians do not want any part of that. When the Minister suggests that 85 per cent of Canadians are on drug plans, he

August 21, 1987
Patent Act
fails to mention that over 1 million Canadians do not have a drug plan. He fails to mention that it is the taxpayer who pays through the nose for the pharmacare program in his or her province.
1 went to law school with an individual who has developed a great legal mind; I will not mention his name. He is now working for the Canadian auto workers union-a great guy. When he appeared before committee and the Members were questioning him he became somewhat insulted with the statement made earlier, and reiterated on that day, that union people should not be worried about C-22, as it does not affect them. He brought an important point to the attention of all Members, and I had hoped-perhaps hoping is too much- that Members opposite would have conceded the point, that when a union is negotiating a package of fringe benefits, whether it is salary, pharmacare, medicare, or whatever, there is only a certain size of pie. If companies have to spend much more money for pharmacare programs, it means there will be less money for the other things that are important to the rank and file union members.
Let me remind all Members that it is union members, through their hard-working constant toil as average working Canadians, who make the biggest contribution to this society. To say to them that they have to pay more for their drugs because the Government wants to see multinational corporations get fatter in profit is, to say the least, a bit unfair.
Why did the government Members on that committee not challenge that witness? Because he was right, that is why they did not challenge him. Now the Government would lead us to believe that it will not affect any Canadian. Although 85 per cent of Canadians are on drug plans paid for by taxpayers' money, over 1 million Canadians do not have a drug plan. Who will pay for them? The rank and file union card-carrying member will have to give up more in terms of bargaining with their employer, if they wish to maintain their pharmacare program with that particular company. Perhaps the Minister of corporate affairs and corporate interests does not refuse, but maybe he does not wish to share that with Members of the House, or indeed the Canadian people.
When we discuss intellectual property rights, let us be cognizant of prices. The Tory Government of Alberta believes there will be higher prices. The Governments of Manitoba, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Ontario believe there will be higher prices. But the Minister states that they are wrong, they do not know anything. They are paying for a pharmaceutical program in their provinces. They come before our committee, and the second Chamber and give evidence. They say that drug prices will rise, but the Minister says, "No, you are wrong. I am right". The Minister of corporate affairs then turns around and says, "But just in case prices do go up, I am going to put $100 million in a sock over here. As the prices go up, you will receive a little compensation". That is pretty nifty. A constituent said to me, that is pretty sleazy.
The difference between the pharmaceutical business and when the Government was attempting to deindex the pensions of senior citizens is that then it was taking it directly. speechtext:
that Bill C-215, an Act to amend the Nuclear Liability Act (limitation period), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Bill C-215, an Act to amend the Nuclear Liability Act, deals specifically with Section 13 of the legislation that passed through this place in 1970, and was proclaimed in 1976. It is a reasonably easy Bill for Members of the House to understand, and it removes 21 words of the section which states:
and in no case shall any such action be brought after ten years from the date
the cause of action arose.
My Bill eliminates those words, which refer to the statutory limitation and which I think I will be able to demonstrate over the next 20 minutes are not in the interest of workers in the nuclear industry or of the Canadian public.
I began work on this Bill six years ago with the Canadian Environmental Law Association. Even though it took six years to reach the floor, I am pleased that it is finally here. I hope that members of the Liberal Party and whichever member of the Government speaks, will allow sufficient time for a vote to be taken on this, so it can go to committee and come back to the House to become law.
Currently there are 22 nuclear reactors operating or under construction in Canada in Ontario, Quebec, and New Brunswick. Bill C-215 is designed for the protection of workers in the nuclear industry, and those who might be advertently or inadvertently exposed to radiation. It is also for the protection of the rights of those who could be exposed should there be an accident at some point in relation to one of our nuclear facilities, or the waste that is stored at various sites in the country.
The legal liability question is an enormous one facing the country. It is presently set at $75 million, which as anybody in the House will know is completely insufficient to deal with even a very small amount of litigation. The 10-year statute of limitation on actions from the date of the cause of action, precludes the overwhelming majority of workers who would be exposed to a long period of low body loadings of radiation, or those who may be exposed to higher doses at some point from taking any action. As we have learned from a variety of studies I will be referring to, most cancers related to the nuclear industry appear more than 10 years after the date of exposure.
Earlier this year the U.S. Congress took this issue very seriously. They voted almost unanimously to raise the liability in relation to U.S. reactors from $705 million U.S. to $7 billion U.S. A recent study commissioned by the U.S. Government and conducted by Sandia National Laboratories found
August 21, 1987

that the possible damage from a nuclear accident in most areas of the United States would likely run in the neighbourhood of $420 billion.
According to the Porter Royal Commission, the risk of a reactor accident in Canada is 100 times higher than the official industry estimates. The likelihood of a Candu accident in our country now runs to about one in every 500 years.
There has been growing concern and focus on this issue. There have been a number of lawsuits that I will be referring to later.
Earlier this year Dr. Harry Griffiths, Chief of Radiology at Toronto General Hospital, swore an affidavit before the Supreme Court of Ontario concluding that radiation from reactors can cause cancer as well as genetic mutation and birth defects.
The benefits of lifting the 10-year statutory limitation are for all Canadians, particularly in providing greater safety for the workers and those who could be exposed as a result of closer scrutiny both by inspectors and other agencies such as the insurance agency.
It would have been great, Mr. Speaker, if there had been no Chernobyl or Three Mile Island. But they have occurred, and it is time for Canada to start conducting the type of scrutiny that has long been required.
One of the documents that I will be referring to is the catalogue of medical effects from Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Although these studies are still incomplete, it is probably the most thorough medical study that has been done in the history of the nuclear age. It catalogues studies of intrauterine effects on children who were born with severe mental retardation, small head size, and so on, beginning at exposures as low as 50 rads. Growth retardation and cataracts have been tracked now for more than 40 years. Cancer and leukemia became noticeable and measurable by about 1950 in relation to those who were being tracked by medical experts. And by 1960, thyroid cancer started to be tracked. A number of other cancers have been tracked and catalogued during the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. It is quite clear from the long-term medical studies that have been done that many types of cancers related to radiation do not appear for 20, 30, or 40 years.
This experience led to an article in the August, 1985 Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. It is a short quotation but it sums up the medical information from Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It reads:
The experience of the atomic bomb survivors presents the most significant
possibility that the exact relation between radiation dose and cancer incidence
can be derived from human data.
A great deal of work has been done in this country recently in articles and other activities by David Poch, a lawyer who works for Energy Probe in Toronto. Mr. Poch made some important observations that were run in The Vancouver Sun on January 20, 1987, and I quote:
Nuclear Liability Act
Union Carbide, CP Rail, and other industrial giants involved in risky business face the sobering reality that if they harm a community or its inhabitants they're on the hook for the damage caused.
That is to be expected. Canadian law-quite sensibly-makes industries liable for their negligence.
But courtesy of our federal government, there is one glaring exception to the rule-the nuclear industry.
Members of this fraternity can lie, cheat, steal, fabricate safety documents and engineering specifications, and knowingly sell faulty products to unsuspecting utilities without facing any civil liability-
To compound the public's protection problems, Canadian insurance companies protect their solvency by excluding coverage for nuclear accidents in every homeowner insurance policy-
An inevitable side effect of the act-
That being the Nuclear Liability Act, Mr. Speaker,
-because it lets the risk makers off the hook-is to remove important incentives to accident prevention. Not only do GE and Westinghouse have less incentive to be careful, but the insurance industry is less likely to scrutinize nuclear companies or to suggest safety improvements, as it does in other sectors.
Mr. Poch has hit the nail on the head as to the problems that are created by having a lack of scrutiny in the industry. The liability limits and the statute of limitations place all of the risks on the communities at large, the workers at large, and the Canadian taxpayers.
The possibility of willful deception is something that has to be addressed. Every other industry in Canada must face the reality that if it damages property and injures or kills Canadians, it is on the hook for the damage caused.
Some excellent studies have been done in relation to various recent nuclear disasters. Of course, the most recent on this continent was the Three Mile Island. Work has been done by a person by the name of Molholt in the United States. There is an excellent quote here in relation to studies that were done by a limited number of people where attempts were made by the nuclear industry and certain state agencies to discredit, but they are now recognized as being accurate. I would like to quote again from an article by David Poch that was published in Harrowsmith. It says:
Molholt's work confirms a doubled infant mortality rate and a tripled neonatal hypothyroid rate in areas downwind. "We took 17 incidents of the metallic taste, burning skin and so on and plotted them against the wind rose-the chart of where the winds were blowing during the worst emissions," Molholt says. "Sixteen of the 17 cases correlated precisely to radiation releases from Three Mile Island. In the long run, it seems, people are the most reliable dosimeters."
Marjorie Aamodt says, "The state held our study a year, doubled our statistical base, did all the manipulating they could and still came up with a cancer rate of almost 2 1/2 times normal."
It is clear that in the United States, the U.S. Congress has at least recognized the need for greater liability coverage. In this country, we have failed to recognize the need for a massive extension of the period within which lawsuits can be brought against an agency responsible for an accident because of the long latency period of cancers. The liability level in the United States was at $75 million. It is now at $7 billion U.S. per reactor. That is certainly an interesting distinction among the

August 21, 1987
Nuclear Liability Act
responses of respective legislatures to the rights of our respective citizens.
Surely industry must be held responsible for the risks that they create for the workers and for the public. Present financial and time limitations are more than just inadequate, they are counter-productive. Risk assessments should be done, for example, by the insurance industry and by federally appointed and hired inspectors who have a much broader and more significant mandate.
The consequences of a nuclear accident are no longer conjecture. As a result of the Chernobyl accident there are 31 dead and medical estimates of 10,000 serious genetic abnormalities and so on.
On May 9 of this year a federal judge in the State of Utah ruled on the U.S. Government's negligence in relation to open air tests of weapons done from 1951 to 1962. The judge, Bruce Jenkins, said the following:
Employees of the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC), working in the 1950's at the Nevada test site, failed to warn the nearby populace adequately about the dangers of fallout exposure. They subsequently failed to monitor the fallout exposure adequately. They also failed to inform the populace adequately about "well-known and inexpensive methods" to minimize the damage once fallout exposure had occurred. "As a direct and proximate result of such negligent failures-(the government) unreasonably placed plaintiffs or their predecessors at risk of injury," the judge said. Only one of the ten cancer victims survived.
On April 27 of this year, precisely one year to the day after the Chernobyl accident, Energy Probe and 11 others filed an application in the Supreme Court of Ontario asking the court to strike down the Nuclear Liability Act for many of the reasons that 1 have put on the record today. I would like to quote the remarks of Norman Rubin on the day of the filing of that suit. He said:
We believe that by reducing or eliminating the nuclear industry's civil liability for accidents, this law removes an important incentive for the industry to reduce the risk of a Canadian Chernobyl. The industry keeps telling us 'It can't happen here,' but they insist on financial protection just in case. We want them to put their money where their mouth is.
Energy Probe alleges that the Nuclear Liability Act reduces security of the person and denies victims of a nuclear accident equality before the law. Joining with Energy Probe in the effort are George Martin from the Nuclear Insurance Association of Canada, Dr. Douglas Alton, staff radiologist from Toronto, Dr. Rosalie Bertell, Dr. Ursula Franklin, Dr. Harry Griffiths, Dr. John Hepburn, Dr. Dermot McLoughlin, Dr. Stan Segel, Dr. Hari Sharma, Dr. David Suzuki and Dr. Lynn Trainor, all of whom have backgrounds in one way or another with chemistry, physics, radiology or genetics. They join in challenging the propriety and appropriateness of the Nuclear Liability Act as it now stands.
The lawyer representing the case is Clayton Ruby, certainly one of Canada's most brilliant and best known barristers. His remarks are worth having on the record as well. I quote:
This law has created one set of rules for the nuclear industry and a different set for everyone else. It allows GE or Westinghouse to supply nuclear plants with defective parts without any financial liability whatsoever should those parts fail and cause an accident. Every other industry is forced to stand behind its products. But in the case of the nuclear industry, where an accident could kill thousands of people and cause billions in property damage, the public has been stripped of its right to its day in court.
In Mr. Ruby's view, this loss of fundamental justice is contrary to Canada's Constitution and should be struck down. Once that happens it is anyone's guess whether the industry will want to stay in operation.
Mr. Ruby continued:
The industry has always claimed the public was irrational to fear reactor accidents, and it may decide to show the world that there's nothing to fear by putting its own money on the line. Or, as 1 think more likely, the nuclear industry will conclude that a serious accident is too likely to bankrupt the industry, and turn its formidable skills to more productive uses.
Even as recently as yesterday we saw what kind of response the nuclear industry makes to concerns raised, even by its own watchdog agency. Earlier this year, in a document drafted by Atomic Energy of Canada, federal regulators made a number of recommendations which are now being pooh-poohed by the nuclear industry as being unnecessary.
However, allow me to point out the following recommendations that were made. The document shows that concerns about the safety of Candu reactors were raised by the Atomic Energy Control Board, the agency charged with watching over Canada's nuclear industry. The document, titled Current Safety and Licensing Issues and presented to a meeting earlier this year, recommended that the Canadian nuclear industry make 13 changes, including additional complex research into reactor behaviour, installation of extra safety equipment, making minor but significant changes to reactor designs, and changing some operating procedures.
For example, the federal regulators are proposing the installation of new equipment to prevent the build-up of hydrogen that they say could cause a fire at the Gentilly-2 reactor operated by Hydro-Quebec and the Point Lepreau reactor operated by New Brunswick Power Corporation.
However, the nuclear industry, through Roger Humphries, an official with Atomic Energy's Candu designed headquarters responds as follows:
If we're going to survive as a commercial entity, we have to be careful not to increase the cost of our product without increasing the safety.
When it comes to the issue of safety, if the regulatory body is making recommendations that it feels are necessary for the safety of the workers in the facility or for the communities nearby, then surely there is an incumbent responsibility on those in charge of the Candu reactor sites to ensure that those changes are promptly and properly implemented, not set aside.
The stall on this rather simple amendment to remove the statute of limitations of 10 years is ludicrous. The workers at those sites are provided with all kinds of protective equipment and the body dose loadings which they get are generally very low and over a very long period of time. The evidence with
August 21, 1987

regard to the latency period of cancers now demonstrates that the kinds of cancers which those workers might get would appear over a very long period of time. That existing clause precludes them from ever having a day in court or any right to financial compensation to assist them or their families in the future.
In terms of accidents it is very clear that that clause should be removed because it would be almost impossible for those exposed at the time of an accident to have their case properly heard before a court. In fact, I agree with the arguments of Mr. Ruby and Energy Probe that the Nuclear Liability Act is contrary to the intent of our Charter.
This matter has been dealt with in a variety of ways, perhaps most energetically by the Canadian Environmental Law Association. However, it has been allowed to lag seriously. 1 have a letter of September of 1981 from Marc Lalonde, the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who wrote to Ms. G. Patterson of the Canadian Environmental Law Association advising CELA that he, as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, supported the proposed change that I am introducing here today, but said the following:
Dear Ms. Patterson:
Thank you for your letter of July 22, 1981 on the subject of revisions to the Nuclear Liability Act. I can assure you that we have not been neglecting this subject and in fact have come to the conclusion that we agree with the intent of your proposed amendment.
However, our experience of operating with this Act for the past five years has shown up other areas where amendment is equally desirable. Discussions have been initiated by the AECB with other affected federal departments aimed at pulling together a complete package of these proposed amendments.
As for the time at which these would be introduced to the House of Commons it would be misleading to be very optimistic when I consider the history of the original Act and the extensive legislation program already ahead of us.
That was six years ago that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his Department agreed that the step about which we are talking today was necessary. If it was necessary six years ago, it is even more necessary today. I think the epidemiological evidence which I have put very briefly before the House, the studies of the effects of Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Chernobyl, Three Mile Island, and the problems that this entire Act faces in being contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, do not leave too many arguments, I would hope, to be dispelled either by the Government or the Liberal Members who might speak.
[DOT] (M20)
I hope that during this hour, we will have an opportunity to vote and send this Bill to committee so that something good can be done for Canadians. I hope we will be able to take something out of a piece of legislation passed by this House in order to make the country safer for the workers and the public generally.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   NUCLEAR LIABILITY ACT MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me to speak on Private Member's Bill C-215 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for
Nuclear Liability Act
Skeena (Mr. Fulton), an Act to amend the Nuclear Liability Act (limitation period).
Those in the House, in my constituency and in the media who know me will be astounded to realize that I have become an instant fresh-frozen expert on nuclear energy. However, that seems to be a lot better than becoming an instantly fresh-fried victim of a nuclear accident.
The survivors of Chernobyl and Three Mile Island know that. Those Canadians, including myself, who are almost frantic about nuclear energy or who have heard and read about its frightening powers, those of us living and of future generations, can well sympathize with the thrust of the Hon. Member's Bill.
As an example of this, the fear of radiation in any form scares the hell out of my own family. Only this past week, I convinced my wife that a microwave oven was safe. As a result, the cubic-foot monster will enter our home later this afternoon.
If my 15-year-old son Liam were standing in my place right now, I am sure he would urge the banning of the entire Atomic Energy Control Board and would shield himself from everyone who comes in contact with the Canadian nuclear industry. I hasten to add that that will not be necessary. 1 hope to assure my son and others that they should not over-react.
I can understand why Canadians might wish to over-react concerning the safety of nuclear energy, but we have come to know both the benefits and the risks of nuclear energy. The benefits of economical, reliable, convenient nuclear-generated electricity must be utilized in cognizance of the related risks, as we have been reminded by the Chernobyl incident. We as legislators must ensure that Canadians enjoy a very favourable risk-benefit balance by providing effective legislation to both ensure the safety and security of nuclear energy and to provide for emergency planning and liability compensation should that ever be required. That is always a concern and a worry.
The Atomic Energy Control Act constitutes and empowers the Atomic Energy Control Board to ensure that nuclear energy is exploited with careful and thorough consideration of the health, safety and security interests of all Canadians. In this respect, the record of the Atomic Energy Control Board and of the regulated Canadian nuclear industry is exemplary. In the unlikely event-and I would urge the Hon. Member for Skeena to listen to that word "unlikely"-that anything should occur in Canada, the Nuclear Liability Act provides the means of compensating Canadians and neighbouring Americans in the case of claims resulting from personal injury and property damage. As the Hon. Member will be aware, since its implementation in 1976, there has not been a single claim made under the Nuclear Liability Act.
The Nuclear Liability Act, as are similar Acts in other nuclear nations, is based on the concept of absolute liability of the nuclear plant operator. The operator is absolutely liable for damages no matter what the cause of the incident giving rise

August 21, 1987
Nuclear Liability Act
to the damages. Such an approach avoids long delays in the addressing of claims as may result from legal proceedings to determine responsibility and liability for the incident giving rise to the damages. This absolute liability extends up to a limit of $75 million for each designated nuclear installation and extends certain time limits with respect to the bringing of claims under the Act.
Such dollar and time limitations are necessary to define clearly the boundaries of the operator's absolute liability. Claims in excess of $75 million give rise to the establishment of a nuclear damage claims commission which addresses such claims and which may recommend their compensation from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. How much more justice could there be for Canadians than that? The absolute liability of the operator and time limitations to that absolute liability were designated to create a liability structure which fairly and effectively serves the interests of both the potential claimant and the nuclear plant operator.
The Nuclear Liability Act provides for several time limitations on the bringing of actions. No person may bring an action for injury or property damage more than three years after the earliest date upon which the person had knowledge or ought reasonably to have had knowledge of the injury or damage. In the case of a claim for loss of life, it may not be brought more than three years after the death of the person. Where conclusive evidence of the death of the person is not available, the claim may not be brought more than three years after a court order is made presuming the person to be dead. However, in no case may a claim be made more than 10 years from the date the cause of action arose.
In summary, there is an absolute limit of 10 years from the time that the damage or injury occurred and a limit of three years from the time a person knew or ought to have known of the injury or damage for the initiation of a claim under the Act. It is the 10-year limitation from the time the damage or injury occurred which is the subject of the Bill we are debating this afternoon.
At issue is the proposition that a 10-year limitation period is not adequate for the manifestation and identification of longer-term radiation-induced injuries such as cancer. Indeed, it is generally accepted and medical experience confirms that a long period of time may elapse between a serious radiation exposure and the manifestation of a radiation-induced injury such as cancer. This period of time may be as long as 30 years or more and is quite likely to exceed the 10-year limitation period currently defined by Section 13 of the Nuclear Liability Act. Consequently, persons who may be injured by radiation exposure resulting from a nuclear incident may be excluded from the bringing of claims by the latency period of the radiation-induced injury such as cancer.
The Hon. Member's Bill proposes not that the 10-year limitation period be extended but rather that it be abolished completely. As such, the proposal overlooks the fact that there must be a fair and just balance struck between the interests of
the injured claimant and those of the absolutely liable nuclear plant operator. Although abolishing the 10-year limitation period would be very much to the advantage of potential claimants, it may significantly and unfairly extend the absolute liability of the nuclear plant operator and leave him in an open-ended situation against which he may not be able to indemnify himself.
In the interests of balance, fairness and justice to the potential claimant and the nuclear plant operator, I believe that the period of limitation should be finite and should be set at 30 years. In view of the current medical knowledge and experience in the field of radiation-induced injury, this would permit injured parties to lay claims in most cases. Should any potential claims be identified after the 30-year period, they would be expected to be very few in number and could be dealt with through the normal court process. Such a 30-year limitation period has already been adopted in several other nuclear liability jurisdictions including West Germany, Austria, Belgium and Denmark. In addition, the U.S. has already increased its absolute liability period from 10 to 20 years and this is expected to increase further in the future to the international norm of 30 years.
I believe we should defeat this motion. I believe a fair, balanced and effective approach would be to extend the current 10-year limitation period to 30 years. It would well serve the interests of both the potential claimant and the nuclear plant operator and would make our legislation consistent with the developing international norm.
Furthermore, and in conclusion, I believe such an amendment would be made as part of an over-all review of the Nuclear Liability Act currently being completed by the interdepartmental working group referred to earlier. Such an approach will ensure that the review and amendment of the Nuclear Liability Act is done in a comprehensive and consistent manner so that the effectiveness of this very important piece of legislation will be enhanced to the greatest possible degree.
I thank the Hon. Member for Skeena for his earlier comments and I thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   NUCLEAR LIABILITY ACT MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to speak on behalf of the amendment suggested by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), and to support it completely.
I welcome the statement made by the government Member who said that the Government favours a 30-year liability period. If the Government is of that mind, then why not send this Bill to committee? If a modification has to be made, I am sure the Hon. Member for Skeena would at least consider it. Anything suggested by the Hon. Member for Hamilton- Wentworth (Mr. Scott) would be preferable to the situation that exists with the Nuclear Liability Act as it presently stands.
August 21, 1987

No one argues with the fact that we have not had a claim under this Act and we all consider ourselves fortunate. However, that is no reason for delaying the protection of Canadians in the future. After all, we have not had a nuclear war yet, but we still have billions of dollars being spent on deterrent forces.
We have to be careful that we do not become blase about the potential danger of a nuclear disaster originating at one of our nuclear stations. Our protection under this Act is woefully inadequate as it presently stands. As the Hon. Member for Skeena said, the maximum liability is $75 million. This is not enough by any stretch of the imagination to protect the safety of Canadians. No one will be able to be compensated adequately if they are injured in any way in a nuclear accident. Surely they are entitled to more protection than the Act presently gives them.
The Hon. Member's motion proposes:
-and in no case shall any such action be brought after ten years from the date the cause of action arose.
I want to speak to that from two points of view. First, the 10-year period is woefully inadequate, as the Hon. Member said. He acknowledged that the Government is considering extending it. In the U.K., for instance, there is a 30-year period. The U.S. has increased it to 20 years or three years from the time the injury became apparent, whichever occurs first. There is now legislation before Congress to remove the 20-year limitation and make it three years from the time the injury became apparent. That is a very significant point. As has been said here today, it may be years before an injury resulting from a nuclear accident becomes apparent. It could be as long as 30 to 40 years according to the testimony of experts in this field. I would say that it is compulsory that we consider this point today and send this Bill to committee.
What is our position in Canada? Not only do we have an inadequate period of time, 10 years, but it is 10 years from the date the cause of action arose. We know it could be 30 or 40 years after the accident before a problem showed itself. Obviously the way it is now is inadequate because people will not have the opportunity to make a claim after they become aware of the injury. Certainly the Government is studying this question, but how long do we have to wait? On May 12 I asked Mr. Robert Blackburn, Director of Planning and Administration Branch of the Atomic Energy Control Board about this and he said:
The Act provides a 10-year limitation period as Mr. MacLellan refers to. This is one of the issues currently being addressed ... It is a generally accepted fact that the latency period for radiation-induced cancer can be considerably longer than 10 years. It could be 30 years in some cases. The interdepartmental working group is very much aware of that. We are making use of the medical information. That is one of the key issues being reviewed and we hope to make a recommendation.
When 1 asked when we could expect such a recommendation he said:
Nuclear Liability Act
We expect to have a report which would include that recommendation before the Atomic Energy Control Board, the five-member board, at its next meeting on June 17.
We are now past that date by over two months and the matter remains unresolved. We cannot continue to have this stalling on this very important matter. We have to come to grips with it. This Bill must go to committee and 1 support the Hon. Member completely.
There are others who have said, "Well, we have limitation periods for all injuries". The statute of limitations says six years. That is for personal injuries which arise through the normal course of events, through unforeseen situations. Here we have a government-sponsored energy creating device which has been put in place in the interests of the Canadian people. This is not a hit or miss situation. This is an organized program. As such, the people of Canada have the right to be completely protected from any ill effects which may arise therefrom.
It is not sufficient, as the Hon. Member for Hamilton- Wentworth said, to say we need a definitive amount so the producers of nuclear power can be assured of a maximum amount for which they would be liable. All nuclear stations in this country are run by Governments. Governments have no right to put a price tag on the safety of Canadians. Governments have an obligation to protect Canadians as much as they possibly can. If something goes amiss, the health of Canadians is put at risk or in fact damaged, then Government has an obligation to compensate these people as much as it possibly can. It is not right to place a maximum of $75 million on that compensation.
We have talked recently about the defects of the Candu system as detected by the Atomic Energy Control Board. We have talked about the fact that AECL has been reluctant to make changes that would fix these defects. In this day and age it is incredible that we would be even having a dialogue about this. They say we have to make changes to correct the defects and we are saying we do not think these changes are necessary. This is all in the spirit of negotiation. It is in the spirit of risking the safety of Canadians, that is what it is. This seems to be the thrust right through the whole piece. The safety of Canadians is not important. Money is more important. Yet money will never compensate Canadians for a nuclear accident.
We have to be cognizant of the fact that such a situation can occur. Not only do Canadians deserve reasonable compensation but it is important that the Government recognize its obligation. Only through doing so with a reasonable liability period and a reasonable maximum liability will the Government take as seriously as it should its obligation to make the nuclear system in Canada as safe as it can possibly be.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speech by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) as well as that given by my colleague. The Hon. Member for

August 21, 1987
Nuclear Liability Act
Skeena quoted a letter by Mr. Ruby of Energy Probe, and quoted another letter in which it is alleged that the suppliers of material for nuclear reactors in Canada and, I assume, in the United States, are lying and deceitful, that the merchandise they are selling is faulty. 1 think those allegations, which were not made by the Member for Skeena, but which he read into the record, are most serious. If he believes that that information and those allegations are correct, then I, as a Member from British Columbia which has a well known stance on nuclear reactors, would urge him to bring that information to the attention of the Minister responsible and, indeed, to all his colleagues in the House. If such an allegation is correct, it means that we are playing with the lives of Canadians and we must either prove or put to rest those allegations once and for all.
The intent of the Bill is to expand the time frame of liability with respect to exposure to radiation. That is not an unusual request. The evidence introduced by the Member for Skeena would suggest that there is a very good read out on that disastrous occurrence at Hiroshima.
I suggest, however, that there is a difference between the radiation impact of that nuclear explosion and the events of Chernobyl or what might flow from a minor but nevertheless deadly leak at some other reactor.
When considering the time factor of 30 or 40 years, we must also consider a number of other factors, including the protective clothing that is worn today. For instance, in the field of radiology in the medical profession, no longer do we see those who use fluoroscopy not wearing protective gloves. The loss of the tips of fingers was not unusual. I had a professor in Toronto who had lost the tips of all his fingers from fluoroscopy.
The blush of blood vessels in the face is another example of what happened to physicians who were not fully aware of the hazards of radiation. The protective apparel worn by physicians and technicians in radiology today has yet to prove whether it is serving its full purpose.
On the other hand, how does one demonstrate that a CA of the lungs or CA of the prostate is due to radiation or due to an aging process, taking into account the age of the patient? We have to understand when that 30-year period will begin, in terms of the age of the patient.
I agree with my colleague that a 30-year limitation is a consideration we should study. I understand that the Government is in fact in the process of discussing that very matter.
Increasingly in Canada, we have come to know both the benefits and risks of nuclear energy. The benefits of economical, reliable, convenient, nuclear-generated electricity must be utilized in cognizance of the related risks. We have been reminded of that by the recent incident at Chernobyl. We as legislators must ensure that Canadians enjoy a very favourable risk-benefit balance by providing effective legislation to both ensure the safety and security of nuclear energy and to provide
for emergency planning and liability compensation should that ever be required.
British Columbia is blessed with an abundance of hydroelectric power and the capacity to generate hydro-electric power by virtue of our massive lakes, rivers, streams and mountains. I believe we are also blessed by the fact that almost unanimously, the people of British Columbia have rejected the nuclear power source.
Of course, that is not always possible in reality. Therefore, we have seen the need for a CANDU reactor in areas of Canada where no other option is available other than thermal generation through coal, which we know produces acid rain.
The Atomic Energy Control Act empowers the Atomic Energy Control Board to ensure that nuclear energy is exploited with careful and thorough consideration of the health, safety and security interests of all Canadians. It is in that respect that I am particularly concerned about the opening remarks of the Hon. Member for Skeena with respect to equipment, parts and parts replacement. In the unlikely event that a major nuclear accident should occur in Canada, the Nuclear Liability Act provides the means of compensating Canadians and neighbouring Americans in the case of claims resulting from personal injury and property damage. Since its implementation in 1976, there has not been a single claim made under the Nuclear Liability Act. One has to be concerned about the limit of $75 million when one considers the possible impact upon the United States. We saw the impact of a combination of bad judgment and ignorance which resulted in that terrible incident at Chernobyl. It displays the possibility that such an accident could have a spill-over effect to another country.
The Hon. Member's Bill proposes not that the 10-year limitation period be extended, but rather that it be abolished completely. As such, the proposal overlooks the fact that there must be a fair and just balance struck between the interests of the injured claimant and those of the absolutely liable nuclear plant operator. Although abolishing the 10-year limitation period would be very much to the advantage of potential claimants, it may significantly and unfairly extend the absolute liability of the nuclear plant operator and leave him in an open-ended situation against which he may not be able to indemnify himself. That is why I made reference to the age of the person when exposure might occur.
I recognize that the Hon. Member's suggestion is a possibility, but a balance must be struck. A possible fair, balanced and effective approach may be to extend the current 10-year limitation period to 30 years. This would well serve the interests of both the potential claimant and the nuclear plant operator and would make our Canadian nuclear liability legislation consistent with the developing international norm. Further, I believe that such an amendment should be made as part of the over-all review of the Nuclear Liability Act currently being completed by the interdepartmental working group, which was referred to earlier. It would be useful for the
August 21, 1987

House to examine carefully the results of that report. Such an approach will ensure that review and amendment of the Nuclear Liability Act is done in a comprehensive and consistent manner so that the effectiveness of this very important piece of legislation will be enhanced to the greatest possible degree.
I thank the Hon. Member for Skeena for drawing this matter to our attention. 1 am confident that the committee will handle this in the most appropriate way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank my colleague from Levis (Mr. Fontaine) for his kindness.
I am very pleased to have this opportunity to debate the Bill of my honourable friend and so-called cousin. The Government acknowledges that a few of the existing provisions of the Nuclear Liability Act are of some concern to various parties. Many Members know that a federal Government interministerial task force is examining some aspects of the legislation. That being so, it would be premature to endorse Bill C-215 at this time.
The Nuclear Liability Act, adopted in 1970 and proclaimed in 1976, provides for funds to offer financial compensation to citizens for injury or damage resulting from an incident in a nuclear plant, a very unlikely occurrence.
The Act alters the normal burden of proof for a claimant by establishing that a duty is owed by the operator, thus eliminating the claimant's need to prove negligence to claim for damages. A claimant need prove only that the injury or damage was caused by the nuclear incident for which the operator is liable, thereby avoiding much unnecessary litigation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, part of the intent of the Act is to ensure that funds are available to provide financial compensation to third parties for injuries or damages suffered as a result of a "nuclear incident". At the same time, the Act provides
Nuclear Liability Act
protection to the operators by limiting their related liability. It limits the total amount payable by the operator in respect of damages arising from a particular nuclear incident to $75 million. Larger amounts may be authorized by Parliament.

In addition, the Nuclear Liability Act protects persons other than operators. For instance, it protects the suppliers of fuel and parts used in nuclear reactors by restricting to the operator any liability due to a nuclear incident and by preventing the operator from taking legal action against these other people with respect to such liability.
When the Governor in Council is of the opinion that it would be in the public interest to provide special measures for compensation following a nuclear incident, Part II of the Act becomes operative and a Nuclear Damage Claims Commission is established. The commission is empowered to examine and settle claims resulting from a nuclear incident and which are transmitted by the Governor in Council.

The Atomic energy Control Board administers the Act. The board designates the nuclear installations that are subject to the Act, determines who is the operator of the nuclear installation by issuing a licence pursuant to the Atomic Energy Control Act, and determines the amount of basic insurance fixed with the approval of the Treasury Board.
At the time it was proclaimed in 1976, the suggestion was made that the Act be reviewed after five years to determine if any changes would be desirable in light of experience in its administration. In 1982, such a review was begun, even though there had not been a claim under the Act.
An interdepartmental working group, as we are aware, consisting of representatives from Justice, Finance, Treasury Board, insurance, Energy, Mines and Resources and the Atomic Energy Control Board first developed a broad-ranging series of questions concerning the Act and then formulated replies to the questions. These replies were not necessarily the final opinion of the working group. However, they were designed to stimulate public response. The resulting consultative document was issued for public comment, and a number of replies were received. None raised questions or issues not already considered by the working group.
As a result of the public input, the working group is currently reconsidering the original series of answers to its questions with a view to making recommendations to the President of the Atomic Energy Control Board later this year.
In its final report, it is likely that the working group will conclude that the Nuclear Liability Act is conceptionally sound and that its purpose and scope are generally still appropriate. However, a number of contentious questions will still have to be addressed, including whether the $75 million limit on the amount of prescribed insurance is still appropriate, and should the limitation period for claims be extended from 10 years to 30 years in order to include cases of delayed

These are fundamental questions which 1 am sure my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena, is most interested to know the answers to.

In their final report the task force will probably conclude that the Nuclear Liability Act was properly drafted and that its purpose and scope generally remain relevant. However a number of contentious questions will have to be answered, for instance:
-Is the $75-million insurance coverage provided under the legislation still adequate?
-Should the 10-year time limit for filing claims be raised to 30 years to take into account latent cancer cases, many of which do not become discernible during the first ten years?

I am sure that Hon. Members of the House will agree that since the matter of extending the current
limitation period for claims set out in the Nuclear Liability Act is already under examination, I say with great regret that it would seem inappropriate to support Bill C-215 at this point in time.
The Minister, I am told, awaits with interest the recommendations of the Atomic Energy Control Board. While it is acknowledged that subsequent recommendations by the board to the Government for amendments to the Act may present concerns to some parties, you can be assured, Mr. Speaker, that the interests and safety of the Canadian public will be of paramount importance throughout this entire process.
